april_fools_day.label: April Fools' Day
april_fools_day.intro: The one day of the year when a well-meant prank is practically expected. Newspapers, brands and families all try to pull off the most convincing nonsense before lunchtime.
funFacts: In France the prank is called poisson d'avril: children try to stick a paper fish on someone's back unnoticed.
In 1957 the BBC showed Swiss farmers harvesting spaghetti from trees, and viewers rang in to ask where to buy a spaghetti bush.
Where the custom began is still unsettled; references to April foolery show up in European writing from the 16th century onwards.

peanut_butter_and_jelly_day.label: National Peanut Butter and Jelly Day
peanut_butter_and_jelly_day.intro: A tribute to the simplest of sandwiches: two slices of bread, peanut butter, a layer of jam. Cheap, sticky and, for millions of people, the taste of childhood.
funFacts: Peanuts are not nuts but legumes, and their pods ripen underground rather than on a branch.
Marcellus Gilmore Edson patented a peanut paste back in 1884, an early ancestor of today's peanut butter.
Sliced bread made the sandwich easy to assemble, and US soldiers are widely credited with spreading the habit in the 1940s.

find_a_rainbow_day.label: National Find a Rainbow Day
find_a_rainbow_day.intro: An invitation to look up after the next shower and hunt for a rainbow. April weather, with its mix of sun and rain, is about as good as the odds ever get.
funFacts: A rainbow is really a full circle; from the ground the horizon hides the lower half, but pilots can see the whole ring.
In a double rainbow the outer arc has its colours in reverse order, with red on the inside.
You can never reach the end of one: the arc forms in the eye of each viewer and moves along as you do.

carrot_day.label: International Carrot Day
carrot_day.intro: A day for the crunchiest vegetable in the drawer, celebrated with carrot cake, carrot soup and raw carrots straight from the bag. It has been marked since 2003.
funFacts: Early cultivated carrots were purple and yellow; orange roots only became the European standard from the 17th century.
Beta-carotene takes its name from the carrot's Latin name carota, and the body converts it into vitamin A.
The longest carrot on record measured 6.245 metres and was grown by Joe Atherton in the UK in 2016.

caramel_day.label: National Caramel Day
caramel_day.intro: Sugar, heat and patience: caramel turns the plainest ingredient in the kitchen into something golden. A good excuse to stir a pan until it smells of toffee.
funFacts: Caramel begins when sugar passes roughly 160 °C and hundreds of new aroma compounds form as it browns.
Add cream and butter and you get soft chewy caramel; keep boiling and the same sugar sets hard as toffee.
Salted caramel became a modern classic after Breton chocolatier Henri Le Roux created his salted-butter caramel in 1977.

tartan_day.label: Tartan Day
tartan_day.intro: Kilts, pipe bands and clan banners: Tartan Day celebrates Scottish heritage in Canada, the US, Scotland and beyond, and it is one of the loudest parades of April.
funFacts: The date recalls the Declaration of Arbroath of 6 April 1320, Scotland's famous letter asserting independence.
After the 1745 rising the Dress Act banned Highland dress in Scotland; the ban was lifted again in 1782.
New York's 2002 Tartan Day parade was led by Sean Connery and included 8,250 pipers and drummers.

international_beaver_day.label: International Beaver Day
international_beaver_day.intro: A day for nature's busiest engineer. Beavers fell trees, dam streams and build whole wetlands, and this date honours the animal and the people who study it.
funFacts: Beavers are the second-largest rodents in the world, beaten only by the capybara.
Their front teeth are orange because iron in the enamel makes them hard enough to gnaw through trunks.
The largest known beaver dam, in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park, is around 850 metres long and was spotted on satellite images.

zoo_lovers_day.label: National Zoo Lovers Day
zoo_lovers_day.intro: For everyone who still gets excited at the penguin enclosure. A day to visit a zoo, watch keepers at work and remember childhood afternoons among the animals.
funFacts: Tiergarten Schönbrunn in Vienna opened in 1752 and is the oldest zoo still operating anywhere in the world.
The short word zoo comes from London's Zoological Gardens, which opened to the general public in 1847.
Przewalski's horse survived only in zoos for decades before breeding programmes returned it to the Mongolian steppe.

unicorn_day.label: National Unicorn Day
unicorn_day.intro: Glitter, rainbows and one impossible horn. Unicorn Day celebrates a creature that never existed and yet turns up on cakes, socks and carousels everywhere.
funFacts: The unicorn is Scotland's national animal and appears in the royal coat of arms.
Medieval traders sold narwhal tusks as unicorn horns, fetching many times their weight in gold.
The Greek physician Ctesias described a one-horned animal in India around 400 BC, one of the oldest written accounts.

siblings_day.label: National Siblings Day
siblings_day.intro: Brothers and sisters get their own date: a day to send an old photo, apologise for something from 1998 and admit that nobody else shares quite the same memories.
funFacts: Claudia Evart founded the day in the US in memory of her siblings and chose the birthday of her sister for the date.
The bond usually lasts longer than any other in life, beginning before friendships and outliving the parents.
Identical twins share almost identical genes but still have completely different fingerprints.

pet_day.label: National Pet Day
pet_day.intro: A day for the animals that share our sofas. Dogs, cats, rabbits, hamsters and everything in between get an extra walk, an extra treat and far too many photos.
funFacts: Dogs were the first domesticated animals; finds in Germany show people and dogs buried together over 14,000 years ago.
A cat's nose print is as individual as a human fingerprint, right down to the pattern of ridges.
Goldfish remember training cues for months, which makes the famous three-second memory a myth.

yuris_night.label: Yuri's Night
yuris_night.intro: Also known as the World Space Party: on 12 April, space fans throw parties, screenings and observatory nights to mark the first human flight into orbit.
funFacts: On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin circled the Earth once in 108 minutes aboard Vostok 1.
Exactly twenty years later, on 12 April 1981, the first Space Shuttle lifted off on its maiden flight.
For the 50th anniversary in 2011 the party ran at more than 567 events in 75 countries on all seven continents.

scrabble_day.label: National Scrabble Day
scrabble_day.intro: The day of the letter tile, held on the birthday of the man who invented the game. Perfect for arguing about whether a word really exists.
funFacts: Architect Alfred Mosher Butts invented the game in the 1930s and first called it Lexiko, then Criss Cross Words.
He worked out the letter frequencies by counting characters on the front page of the New York Times.
Only four S tiles are in the bag: too many would have made plurals an easy way out of every tight spot.

dolphin_day.label: National Dolphin Day
dolphin_day.intro: Clever, curious and permanently grinning: a day for dolphins, the marine mammals that surf bow waves and seem to enjoy an audience.
funFacts: Dolphins sleep with one half of the brain at a time so they keep surfacing to breathe.
Every bottlenose dolphin develops a signature whistle that works like a name and gets answered by others.
The orca is not really a whale in the narrow sense but the largest member of the dolphin family.

world_art_day.label: World Art Day
world_art_day.intro: Held on Leonardo da Vinci's birthday, World Art Day invites everyone into museums, studios and open workshops, and encourages people to simply pick up a brush.
funFacts: The date is Leonardo da Vinci's birthday: he was born on 15 April 1452 near Vinci in Tuscany.
The International Association of Art launched the day in 2012, and UNESCO adopted it as a world day in 2019.
The Mona Lisa has no eyebrows, one of the small oddities visitors queue in the Louvre to check for themselves.

eggs_benedict_day.label: National Eggs Benedict Day
eggs_benedict_day.intro: Toasted muffin, ham, a poached egg and a spoonful of hollandaise: the most luxurious way to eat breakfast, and a dish that brunch menus refuse to give up.
funFacts: Two New York stories compete for the invention: Delmonico's restaurant and a hangover order at the Waldorf in 1894.
Hollandaise is an emulsion of egg yolk and butter; if it splits, a splash of cold water often brings it back.
Poaching works without the shell in barely simmering water, and a dash of vinegar helps the white set quickly.

bat_appreciation_day.label: International Bat Appreciation Day
bat_appreciation_day.intro: Spring is when bats leave their winter roosts, so mid-April is a fitting moment to appreciate the only mammals that truly fly and the insects they clear from our evenings.
funFacts: Bats are the only mammals capable of powered flight; everything else that glides is merely falling with style.
There are more than 1,400 bat species, which makes roughly one in five mammal species a bat.
The bumblebee bat weighs about two grams and is considered the smallest mammal in the world.

pinata_day.label: National Piñata Day
pinata_day.intro: Blindfold, stick, three turns and swing: the piñata turns any party into a small competition. A day for papier-mâché animals filled with sweets.
funFacts: The classic star piñata has seven points, which originally stood for the seven deadly sins.
The oldest versions were clay pots; today most piñatas are papier-mâché built over a balloon.
Similar smashing customs existed in Europe and in China long before the piñata became a Mexican fixture.

garlic_day.label: National Garlic Day
garlic_day.intro: A day for the bulb that quietly improves almost every savoury dish on earth, and that people have been growing, plaiting and hanging up for thousands of years.
funFacts: Garlic only smells once it is damaged: cutting or crushing turns a precursor compound into pungent allicin.
According to Herodotus, the workers who built the pyramids were rationed garlic and onions.
Gilroy in California calls itself the garlic capital and its festival famously served garlic ice cream.

pineapple_upside_down_cake_day.label: National Pineapple Upside-Down Cake Day
pineapple_upside_down_cake_day.intro: Baked bottom up in a skillet and flipped onto the plate, so caramelised pineapple rings and glacé cherries end up on top. A retro cake that never really left.
funFacts: The cake bakes with the fruit underneath, and only the flip at the end puts the caramelised rings on show.
It became a household name after a 1925 recipe contest for canned pineapple that drew around 60,000 entries.
Pineapples do not grow on trees: each low bromeliad plant produces just one fruit at a time.

bulldogs_are_beautiful_day.label: Bulldogs Are Beautiful Day
bulldogs_are_beautiful_day.intro: Wrinkled face, broad chest, unhurried walk: the bulldog will never win a beauty contest — which is exactly the point today. A day for the most charming squashed nose around.
funFacts: The breed goes back to dogs bred for bull-baiting; Britain banned the spectacle in 1835.
Over 80 per cent of bulldog litters are delivered by caesarean, because the heads are so large.
Yale University has had a bulldog mascot called Handsome Dan since 1889.

jelly_bean_day.label: National Jelly Bean Day
jelly_bean_day.intro: Small, shiny and impossible to eat just one of: jelly beans get their own day, ideally poured into a jar so the colours can be sorted before eating.
funFacts: The glossy shell comes from panning, a slow coating technique also used for sugared almonds.
Ronald Reagan loved them so much that a blue variety was created for his 1981 inauguration.
Making them takes days: the chewy centre is moulded and dried before layer after layer of syrup and sugar goes on.

german_beer_day.label: German Beer Day
german_beer_day.intro: Germany raises a glass to its brewing tradition on the anniversary of the 1516 purity law, from wheat beer in the south to pilsner in the north.
funFacts: On 23 April 1516 the Bavarian dukes decreed in Ingolstadt that beer should contain only barley, hops and water.
Yeast was missing from that list simply because nobody knew it existed yet.
German brewers have marked the day since 1995, and around 1,500 breweries are still at work in the country.

pigs_in_a_blanket_day.label: National Pigs in a Blanket Day
pigs_in_a_blanket_day.intro: Little sausages wrapped in dough, served warm from the tray. The party snack that disappears fastest gets a day of its own.
funFacts: In the US they are cocktail sausages in pastry; in Britain the name means sausages wrapped in bacon at Christmas.
The first printed recipe under this name appeared in a Betty Crocker cookbook for children in 1957.
German kitchens make a close relative called Würstchen im Schlafrock, sausages in a dressing gown of dough.

world_penguin_day.label: World Penguin Day
world_penguin_day.intro: Tuxedos, waddling and belly slides: late April is when Adélie penguins head north, and the date has become a worldwide celebration of penguins in general.
funFacts: There are around 18 penguin species, all in the southern hemisphere, though the Galápagos penguin reaches the equator.
Emperor penguins dive more than 500 metres deep and can stay under water for over 20 minutes.
The date is tied to the annual northward migration of Adélie penguins away from their Antarctic colonies.

pretzel_day.label: National Pretzel Day
pretzel_day.intro: Knotted, glossy and sprinkled with coarse salt: the pretzel gets its own day. Whether Bavarian Breze or soft American street pretzel, the shape is unmistakable.
funFacts: Before baking, a pretzel takes a short bath in lye, which is what gives it the dark, shiny crust.
The Bavarian Breze has been registered as a protected geographical indication since 2014.
Philadelphia counts as the pretzel capital of the US, where people eat many times the national average.

gummy_bear_day.label: National Gummi Bear Day
gummy_bear_day.intro: A day for the chewiest bears in the world. Gummi bears started out in a German kitchen and now come in every colour, flavour and questionable shape imaginable.
funFacts: Hans Riegel invented the gummi bear in Bonn in 1922; the original Tanzbär was taller and slimmer than today's version.
The brand name HARIBO is simply short for Hans Riegel Bonn.
Classic gummi bears are made mostly of glucose syrup, sugar and gelatine, which gives them their bounce.

superhero_day.label: National Superhero Day
superhero_day.intro: Capes, masks and impossible landings: a day for comic-book heroes and for the everyday people we quietly call heroes too.
funFacts: Superman appeared in Action Comics #1 in 1938 and is regarded as the first modern superhero.
Wonder Woman followed in 1941, created by psychologist William Moulton Marston, co-inventor of an early lie detector.
The trademark on the term Super Hero was held jointly by Marvel and DC for decades, an unusual arrangement between rivals.

international_dance_day.label: International Dance Day
international_dance_day.intro: Ballet, breakdance, tango or kitchen disco: the day celebrates every form of dance and opens studios and stages to anyone willing to move.
funFacts: The date honours Jean-Georges Noverre, born on 29 April 1727 and the great reformer of ballet.
The International Theatre Institute launched the day in 1982, and each year a dance figure writes the official message.
The waltz was considered scandalous around 1800 because the couples held each other so closely while turning.

international_jazz_day.label: International Jazz Day
international_jazz_day.intro: The last day of April belongs to jazz: clubs, schools and orchestras around the world play together, improvise and close Jazz Appreciation Month in style.
funFacts: UNESCO proclaimed the day in 2011, and pianist Herbie Hancock hosted the first edition in 2012.
Well over 100 countries take part, with a global concert staged in a different host city each year.
Jazz is usually traced to New Orleans around 1900, where blues, ragtime and brass bands came together.
